intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that cleft lip/palate-ectodermal dysplasia syndrome (CLPED1) is caused by homozygous mutation in the PVRL1 gene on chromosome 11q23. Heterozygosity for a PVRL1 mutation has been associated with sporadic nonsyndromic cleft lip/palate (OFC7).

checks.evidence_quote: Cleft lip/palate-ectodermal dysplasia syndrome is a rare, autosomal recessive disorder caused by homozygous loss-of-function mutations of the poliovirus receptor-like 1 (PVRL1) gene encoding nectin-1.

paragraphs.text: Cleft lip/palate-ectodermal dysplasia syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder. Its features include cleft lip/palate, ectodermal dysplasia affecting the hair, teeth, and nails, cutaneous syndactyly of the fingers and/or toes, and a distinctive facial appearance. Some patients also have mental retardation (Suzuki et al., 1998; Yoshida et al., 2015).

paragraphs.text: Bustos et al. (1991) described 27 affected individuals from 7 families that were very probably related to one another. The families lived in a relatively isolated, inbred population with very small neighboring communities on Margarita Island, in Nueva Esparta State in northeastern Venezuela. Affected individuals had ectodermal dysplasia and other anomalies. Females were affected as severely as males, and expressivity was variable. All parents were normal. The authors could not classify the condition among the known ectodermal dysplasias and considered it a newly recognized dysplasia/malformation syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Yoshida et al. (2015) reported a 7-year-old Japanese boy who was the first child of a consanguineous marriage. He had hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia with sparse, brittle, fine, dry hair and hypodontia. He also had a distinctive facial appearance with cleft lip/palate, cutaneous syndactyly of the fingers, and mild mental retardation. Scanning electron microscopy of the hair showed pili torti and pili trianguli et canaliculi.

paragraphs.text: Zlotogora et al. (1987) concluded that the syndrome was most probably inherited as an autosomal recessive disorder, based on its occurrence in 2 sibs. Oğur and Yüksel (1988) and Rodini and Richieri-Costa (1990) reported affected sibs born to consanguineous parents. Bustos et al. (1991) observed 7 inbred Margarita Island families with normal parents and equal severity in females and males. They concluded that the disorder is an autosomal recessive syndrome. Yoshida et al. (2015) found a homozygous PVRL1 mutation in a child of consanguineous parents, and both parents were heterozygous for the mutation.

paragraphs.text: Suzuki et al. (2000) used positional cloning to identify PVRL1 as the gene responsible for CLPED1. PVRL1 encodes nectin-1, an immunoglobulin-related transmembrane cell-cell adhesion molecule that is part of the NAP cell adhesion system. They identified PVRL1 mutations in CLPED families from Margarita Island, Israel, and Brazil. In animal studies, PVRL1 was expressed in the medial edge epithelium of the palatal shelves and in the skin surface epithelium, sites that corresponded to the clinical features of CLPED.

paragraphs.text: Yoshida et al. (2015) studied a Japanese boy with CLPED1 who was the child of consanguineous parents (see Clinical Features). Analysis of exon 2 of PVRL1 showed a novel homozygous nonsense mutation, c.400C-T (R134X). Both parents were heterozygous for the mutation. The authors noted that all 4 PVRL1 mutations reported in CLPED1 up to that time, including this one, produce truncated proteins that lack the transmembrane and intracellular domains of nectin-1. These domains are needed to initiate cell-cell adhesion.

checks.claim: Yoshida et al. (2015) studied a 7-year-old Japanese boy with CLPED1 who was born to consanguineous parents.
checks.evidence_quote: A 7-year-old Japanese boy, the first child of a consanguineous marriage

checks.claim: The Japanese boy with CLPED1 studied by Yoshida et al. (2015) had hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia and cleft lip/palate.
checks.evidence_quote: showed hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia with sparse, brittle, fine, dry hair and hypodontia, the unique facial appearance with cleft lip/palate

checks.claim: The Japanese boy with CLPED1 studied by Yoshida et al. (2015) had cutaneous syndactyly of the fingers and mild mental retardation.
checks.evidence_quote: cutaneous syndactyly of the fingers and mild mental retardation

checks.claim: Analysis of PVRL1 exon 2 in the Japanese boy studied by Yoshida et al. (2015) showed a homozygous c.400C-T transition resulting in an arg134-to-ter (R134X) substitution.
checks.evidence_quote: Mutation analysis of exon 2 of PVRL1 revealed a novel homozygous nonsense mutation, c.400C>T (p.Arg134*).
checks.explanation: Equivalent notation. A C>T change is a transition.

checks.claim: Both parents of the Japanese boy studied by Yoshida et al. (2015) were heterozygous for the PVRL1 R134X mutation.
checks.evidence_quote: His parents were heterozygous for the mutant alleles.

checks.claim: The predicted truncated protein from PVRL1 R134X lacks the transmembrane and intracellular domains of nectin-1.
checks.evidence_quote: All four PVRL1 mutations identified in cleft lip/palate-ectodermal dysplasia syndrome to date, including this study, resulted in truncated proteins that lack the transmembrane domain and intracellular domain of nectin-1
checks.explanation: Stated directly; the four mutations include this one.
